q: Carmignano's historical distinction predates every Super Tuscan. Explain.
accept: cosimo iii 1716 delimitation first doc to require cabernet 1975
ans: Cosimo III de' Medici delimited it in 1716 — one of the world's first appellations (with Chianti, Pomino, Val d'Arno di Sopra) — and 'uva francesca' (Cabernet) has grown there since the Medici era; at DOC in 1975 it became the first Italian appellation to REQUIRE Cabernet in the blend, DOCG 1990.
exp: The 1716 bando delimited zones, not grapes — the legal Super Tuscan precedent is the 1975 DOC.

q: Name Lazio's revived white grape of Frascati and its historical papal trap.
accept: malvasia del lazio puntinata est est est montefiascone
ans: Malvasia del Lazio (puntinata); the 'Est! Est!! Est!!!' legend belongs to Montefiascone's bishop's servant
exp: Trebbiano bulks the blend; the Malvasia carries the perfume.

q: Which Sicilian fortified wine did Marco De Bartoli refuse to fortify, and what did he call it?
accept: vecchio samperi unfortified marsala style perpetuum
ans: Vecchio Samperi — an unfortified, solera-aged Grillo in the ancestral Marsala style (sold outside the DOC)
exp: He was prosecuted and vindicated; the bottle is a manifesto.

q: Etna's contrada system compares to which French model, and name three famous contrade.
accept: burgundy climats guardiola rampante calderara sottana feudo di mezzo
ans: Burgundy's climats; e.g., Guardiola, Rampante, Calderara Sottana, Santo Spirito, Feudo di Mezzo
exp: Altitude bands (400–1,000 m) matter as much as the lava flow's age.

q: Pantelleria's viticulture is UNESCO-listed for which practice?
accept: alberello pantesco head trained vines in hollows
bush vines in pits against wind
ans: Alberello pantesco — head-trained bush vines grown in hollows against ferocious wind (UNESCO Intangible Heritage, 2014)
exp: Zibibbo (Muscat of Alexandria) for Passito di Pantelleria.

ans: Fiano di Avellino (with Greco di Tufo the pair)
exp: Fiano's Latin name 'vitis apiana' — the vine of bees, drawn by its sweetness.

q: Sardinia's Cannonau, Carignano del Sulcis and Vermentino di Gallura — give each its status quirk.
accept: cannonau grenache carignano ungrafted sand vermentino gallura only docg
ans: Cannonau = Grenache (claimed Sardinian-origin by some studies); Carignano del Sulcis grows ungrafted on sand; Vermentino di Gallura is Sardinia's only DOCG
exp: The ungrafted-sand answer recurs from Colares to Lodi.

q: Explain the 'Consorzio' function in Italian wine and one power it holds.
accept: producers association sets rules promotes controls yields can raise standards
ans: A producers' consortium administers the disciplinare — proposing rule changes, controlling yields, promoting the appellation, and (erga omnes) binding all producers
exp: Chianti Classico's consorzio created Gran Selezione and the UGAs by vote.

q: Explain how Vin Santo del Chianti Classico is made, and what the madre contributes.
accept: grapes are dried into winter then pressed into small sealed caratelli and aged in the attic with the madre
appassimento then years in sealed barrels in the vinsantaia where the madre is the old lees culture
dried grapes fermented very slowly in caratelli with a lees starter for at least two years in wood
trebbiano and malvasia air dried pressed and sealed into casks through summer and winter
ans: Trebbiano Toscano and Malvasia Bianca Lunga, at least 60% of the blend together - or a minimum 80% Sangiovese for the Occhio di Pernice version - are dried after harvest, on cane mats or hung from rafters in a ventilated loft, until the fruit reaches at least 27% sugar, which in practice means pressing in winter rather than autumn. The shrivelled grapes are pressed to a syrupy must and run into caratelli, casks of no more than 300 litres (3 hl), usually oak or chestnut, filled only part way and sealed with cement, wax or clay. They sit in the vinsantaia, an unheated attic that bakes in summer and freezes in winter, and the wine ferments in fits and starts across the years as the temperature swings, with no topping up and no racking. The madre is the residue of lees left in the cask from the previous cycle, or added from another: it carries a stress-hardened, alcohol- and sugar-tolerant yeast population capable of working at extreme Brix, and it is the source of a house's continuity of character, passed down cask by cask. The wine must spend at least 24 months in caratelli, counted from 1 January after the harvest, and cannot be released before 1 November of the third year following the vintage - Occhio di Pernice included.
exp: The two things candidates get wrong: that the cask is sealed and deliberately never topped, so oxidation and heat are the recipe rather than faults; and that Vin Santo is not necessarily sweet - it runs from bone dry through amabile depending on where the yeast finally surrenders. The madre is the closest thing in Italian wine to a sourdough starter. Note too that the famous 1 December pressing date belongs to Vin Santo di Carmignano and Vin Santo di Montepulciano; the Chianti Classico rule is a sugar target instead.

q: Compare Aglianico as grown in Taurasi, Aglianico del Taburno and Aglianico del Vulture.
accept: taurasi is the most structured taburno is limestone clay and rounder vulture is volcanic and mineral
irpinia benevento and basilicata with vulture superiore as the docg tier
three aglianico appellations differing by altitude soil and ageing requirement
taurasi docg aglianico del taburno docg and aglianico del vulture superiore docg compared
ans: Taurasi, in Irpinia east of Avellino, sits at roughly 400 to 700 metres on clay with volcanic influence; harvest runs into late October and November, and the wine is the most structured and longest-lived of the three - a minimum of 85% Aglianico, three years' ageing with one in wood, four for Riserva. Aglianico del Taburno, DOCG since 2011, lies on the limestone-clay slopes of Monte Taburno in Benevento, with cooler nights and a slightly earlier harvest; the wines are firm but rounder, more red-fruited and less monumental than Taurasi, and the zone is still the region's underpriced one. Aglianico del Vulture, in Basilicata, grows on the black volcanic soils of an extinct volcano at around 450 to 600 metres, where the DOC is Aglianico del Vulture and Superiore is the DOCG tier; the wines are darker, ash-inflected and more overtly mineral, with riper fruit and tannin no less severe. Across all three, the variety's signature holds: very late ripening, high acid and high tannin together, and a wine that genuinely needs a decade in a way few southern Italian reds do.
exp: This is a lesson in soil and altitude rather than grape - the same variety, three geologies, three answers. Mastroberardino kept Taurasi alive through the twentieth century, and Vulture's revival came later and from fewer hands. Aglianico ripens later than any other major Italian red, which is why every one of these zones is high and inland.

q: Trace the Barolo Wars: the two camps, their techniques, and the reconciliation.
accept: modernists rotofermenters barriques traditionalists botti long maceration converged
gaja altare voerzio versus mascarello rinaldi conterno
ans: Modernists (Altare, Voerzio, Sandrone): short rotofermenter macerations, barriques, early approachability. Traditionalists (Bartolo Mascarello, Rinaldi, Giacomo Conterno): long submerged-cap macerations, Slavonian botti. The 2000s converged on long maceration with judicious large oak
exp: Ask a Piemontese today and both sides claim they won.

q: Name Barbaresco's four MGA aristocrats and their commune.
accept: asili rabaja martinenga montefico montestefano barbaresco neive
ans: e.g., Asili, Rabajà, Martinenga (Barbaresco commune), Montefico/Montestefano; Santo Stefano and Gallina in Neive
exp: Martinenga is Marchesi di Grésy's monopole — the appellation's only one.

q: Explain 'sorì' and 'bricco' in Piedmontese vineyard vocabulary.
accept: sori south facing slope where snow melts first bricco ridge crest
ans: Sorì: the south-facing slope where snow melts first; bricco: the ridge crest or hilltop
exp: Gaja's Sorì San Lorenzo and Sorì Tildìn wear the dialect as branding.

q: Amarone's appassimento loss and legal minimum drying period:
accept: grapes lose a third of weight dried to december
ans: ~30–40% weight loss over roughly 100+ days; grapes may not be pressed before December 1 of the harvest year
exp: Fruttai lofts with fans replaced open attics after the 2000s rot scares.

q: What is the 'Valpolicella pyramid' from base to apex, and where does Ripasso sit?
accept: valpolicella classico superiore ripasso amarone recioto
ans: Valpolicella → Classico/Superiore → Ripasso (refermented on Amarone pomace) → Amarone → Recioto (sweet apex)
exp: Ripasso earned its own DOC in 2010 — 'baby Amarone' as legal category.
